subtype: Approach: working backward from the audience's need [Thinking]
passage: Faculty guide's note, project review week. Lakshmi and Pallavi came to me with forty slides for a fifteen-minute talk. Before I said anything, Lakshmi put the deck aside and asked aloud, "What does the panel actually have to decide on Friday? Whether the sensor is ready to be tested in a real field. That is all." Pallavi objected that the survey work would be wasted. Lakshmi replied, "It stays in the report. On stage it only matters if it helps them say yes." Together they rebuilt the talk around one message and kept nine slides. I asked nothing more, but I saw that the talk now had a spine, and both students were calmer than a week ago.

qa.q: How many slides did Lakshmi and Pallavi keep for the talk?
qa.a: They kept nine slides for the talk.

qa.q: What was Pallavi worried about when Lakshmi set the deck aside?
qa.a: Pallavi was worried that the survey work would be wasted, though Lakshmi explained that it would stay in the report.

qa.q: What alternative approach could help if the panel wants to see more data?
qa.a: They could prepare a few backup slides and show them only if asked, because the main talk stays short while the extra evidence is ready.

qa.q: How might a panel member see a talk built on one message?
qa.a: A panel member could find it easier to decide, since the talk answers the question the panel came to settle.

grounding: Students ask what the panel must decide and build a short talk around one message rather than showing all their work.

passage: Design tutor's note, Wednesday. Before opening any software, Tejas asked for a stack of blank cards and a marker. Naveen watched from the next bench. On each card Tejas drew a rough box and gave it a job: the problem, the method, the result, the next step. Twelve cards went on the table. Then came the cutting. "Does this one help tell the story?" Tejas asked, and four cards went into the bin, including a pretty diagram that led nowhere. The cards were moved around twice. Only after that did the laptop come out, and the slides took forty minutes. I did not give advice. I only noticed that the slides matched the cards exactly, and that Naveen asked to try the same method next week.

qa.q: How many cards went on the table, and how many were thrown away?
qa.a: Twelve cards went on the table, and four went into the bin.

qa.q: What was Tejas thinking when asking whether a card helped tell the story?
qa.a: Tejas wanted every slide to serve the story and was willing to throw away even a pretty diagram that led nowhere.

qa.q: What other approach could Tejas use if the story still feels unclear, and why?
qa.a: Tejas could tell the card sequence aloud to a friend, because gaps in the story show up quickly when someone listens.

qa.q: How might Naveen see the paper stage compared with opening the software straight away?
qa.a: Naveen saw a quicker and clearer route, so much so that Naveen asked to try the same method next week.

grounding: A student sketches each slide on paper as problem, method, result and next step, and cuts every slide that does not serve the story.

subtype: Approach: rehearsing aloud with a timer [Action]
passage: The final review was at ten the next morning, and Pradeep sat in the flat with a stopwatch, a bottle of water and the printed slides. First run: fourteen minutes. Second run, with a slide removed: twelve. Pradeep noticed that the middle, the part on data cleaning, ate most of the extra time. Jahnavi came over after dinner and listened to the third run from the sofa, and said the middle was where her attention drifted. Pradeep cut two sentences and one chart. The last run ended at nine minutes fifty seconds. Pradeep wrote the time on a sticky note and stuck it to the laptop lid, glad to know exactly how long the talk would last.

qa.q: How long did the final run of the talk take?
qa.a: The last run ended at nine minutes fifty seconds.

qa.q: What did Pradeep feel when the last run fit the time?
qa.a: Pradeep felt glad to know exactly how long the talk would last. 🙂

qa.q: What could Pradeep try next to be safe on the morning, and why?
qa.a: Pradeep could do one more run in the review room or with a friend standing, since the real room feels different from a sofa.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi see the feedback she gave?
qa.a: Jahnavi probably feels useful, because her honest remark that her attention drifted showed Pradeep exactly which part to shorten.

grounding: A student rehearses aloud with a timer, once before a friend, trims to the limit and notices which section runs long.

subtype: Approach: putting all text on slides and reading it out [Pitfall]
passage: In the seminar hall on the second floor, Rafiq stood at the lectern as the projector warmed up. Every slide was full: whole paragraphs in small type, copied from the report because Rafiq was afraid of losing the thread. Rafiq began to read from the screen, word for word, with eyes turned to the wall. By slide three the audience had already read ahead. Nikita, in the second row, stopped taking notes. A lecturer glanced at the wristwatch. Someone yawned. A student asked a question about a point three slides back, since nobody could recall what had been said. Rafiq finished four minutes early and looked at the floor. The clapping was polite and short.

qa.q: Where did Rafiq stand when the projector warmed up?
qa.a: Rafiq stood at the lectern in the seminar hall on the second floor.

qa.q: What was Rafiq afraid of when filling the slides with paragraphs?
qa.a: Rafiq was afraid of forgetting what to say and losing the thread, so the report text went onto every slide.

qa.q: What could Rafiq try next time instead of reading the slides, and why?
qa.a: Rafiq could keep a few words on each slide and practise saying the rest, because the audience listens to a speaker but reads faster than anyone can talk.

qa.q: How did Nikita and the audience experience the talk?
qa.a: Nikita and others read ahead, lost interest and stopped taking notes, so nobody remembered what had been said.

grounding: A student fills slides with paragraphs out of fear and reads them aloud, and the audience loses interest.

subtype: Approach: pre-mortem on what could go wrong [Thinking]
passage: Nikita asked, "Pranav, what do you do the night before?" Well, I sit down with a notebook and tell myself, imagine it went badly, what happened? Three things came up. The projector could die. Someone might ask a question I can't answer. Or my mind could go completely blank. So I fixed each one. A printed copy of the slides in my bag. A short answer written for the question I feared most, about sample size. And a rule for the blank moment: stop, breathe once, look at the notes, and carry on. On the day the projector really did flicker, and I just held up the paper and kept talking. Expecting the trouble made it small, Nikita, and I wasn't shaken.

qa.q: What three problems did Pranav imagine the night before?
qa.a: Pranav imagined that the projector could die, that someone might ask a question Pranav could not answer, and that Pranav's mind could go blank.

qa.q: How did Pranav feel when the projector flickered on the day?
qa.a: Pranav was not shaken, because the printed copy meant the trouble had already been expected.

qa.q: What could Pranav add to this plan, and why?
qa.a: Pranav could also ask for the room key early to test the cable and screen, since checking the setup avoids some failures completely.

qa.q: How might Nikita, hearing this, see the fear of giving talks?
qa.a: Nikita may see stage fear as something to prepare for, since Pranav's plan turns a vague worry into three small tasks.

grounding: A student imagines the projector failing, a hard question or a blank moment and prepares a printed copy, an answer and a breathing pause.

subtype: Approach: mental simulation of the room [Thinking]
passage: My name is Amandeep, and the night before my final-year talk I lay on the bed and did something odd. I pictured the seminar hall: the long table, the panel with their pens, the clicker in my hand. Then I saw the first minute. I walk in, say good morning, and open with one sentence, the one I had written on a card. I heard my own voice in the empty room. I did it three times. Saurabh called that evening and asked if I was terrified. I said, "Less than I expected." The morning felt strangely familiar, as if I had been there once already, and my first sentence came out steady.

qa.q: What did Amandeep picture the night before the talk?
qa.a: Amandeep pictured the seminar hall with the long table, the panel, the clicker and the first minute of the talk.

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel when walking in on the morning?
qa.a: Amandeep felt that it was strangely familiar and less frightening than expected, as if it had already been visited once. 🙂

qa.q: What else could Amandeep do to prepare, and why?
qa.a: Amandeep could visit the empty hall the day before and stand where the talk will happen, since a real look makes the picture more exact.

qa.q: How might Saurabh see Amandeep's calm on the phone call?
qa.a: Saurabh may be surprised and reassured, since Amandeep said the fear was less than expected.

grounding: The night before, a student pictures the hall, the first minute and the opening sentence, which makes the first minute feel familiar.

subtype: Approach: winging it because of confidence in the topic [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Shankar, and I know this project inside out, which is why I skipped the rehearsal. My friend Gautam asked if I'd like to run through it. I said, "I'll just talk, I know it." On the day I began well, then wandered into the story of how the dataset was collected, then into a side note on the tools, then a joke that took a full minute. The panel chair raised a hand and said we had time for two more minutes. My main result, the whole reason for the work, was still on slide nine. I got cut off at slide five. Walking out, I understood that knowing the topic is not the same as knowing the talk.

qa.q: At which slide was Shankar cut off?
qa.a: Shankar was cut off at slide five.

qa.q: Why did Shankar skip the rehearsal Gautam offered?
qa.a: Shankar felt sure that knowing the project well was enough, and said just talking would be fine.

qa.q: What could Shankar do differently next time, and why?
qa.a: Shankar could time one full run and choose the result to say first, because a rehearsal shows where the talk wanders.

qa.q: How might the panel chair have seen the talk?
qa.a: The panel chair probably felt frustrated and pressed for time, since the main result never arrived within the limit.

grounding: A student who knows the project well skips rehearsal, rambles past the time limit and is cut off before reaching the main result.

subtype: Approach: anticipating questions with a friend [Action]
passage: Sahil booked the small meeting room in the hostel for Saturday evening. Madhav had agreed to play the tough examiner and had brought a list of questions written on the back of an old timetable. "Why this dataset and not a larger one?" "How do you know the result is not by chance?" "What would you do with more time?" Five in all. After each one, Sahil wrote an answer in a couple of lines. Two questions were easy. Two took a while to answer well. One, about the method's limits, could not be answered at all. Sahil marked it in red and put it on Sunday's reading list. They ended with tea, and Madhav gave a sober thumbs up.

qa.q: How many questions did Madhav ask?
qa.a: Madhav asked five questions in all.

qa.q: What was Sahil probably feeling when the question on the method's limits could not be answered?
qa.a: Sahil probably felt a bit uneasy but honest, since the question was marked in red and put on the reading list.

qa.q: What other approach could help Sahil practise, and why?
qa.a: Sahil could also answer the questions aloud to a phone recorder, because hearing the answers shows which sound unclear.

qa.q: How might Madhav see the role of tough examiner?
qa.a: Madhav is helping Sahil find weak spots early, and probably feels useful while doing it.

grounding: A friend acts as a tough examiner and asks five questions, and the student writes short answers and notes what needs more reading.

passage:
Usha: Nervous?

Pooja: A bit. My voice always shakes right after the first slide. Every single time.

Usha: So what will you do?

Pooja: When it happens, I'll slow down. Stop for a second. Sip water. Carry on.

Usha: You've planned for it?

Pooja: Yes. Nerves are normal. I can't switch them off, but I can handle them.

(later, at the lectern)

Pooja: Let me pause here for a moment.

Usha, whispering: You've got this.

Pooja: Thank you. Right, where was I? The second slide shows the results.

Usha, afterwards: Your voice steadied within a minute.

Pooja: Because I didn't fight it. I let it pass.

qa.q: What did Pooja say would happen right after the first slide?
qa.a: Pooja said that the voice always shakes right after the first slide.

qa.q: What did Pooja feel about the shaking voice before the talk?
qa.a: Pooja was a bit nervous but calm about it, as nerves were expected and had a plan.

qa.q: What could Pooja try if the pause does not calm the voice, and why?
qa.a: Pooja could slow the pace of speaking even more and look at one friendly face, since a steady breath and pace often settle a shaky start.

qa.q: How might Usha see Pooja's pause at the lectern?
qa.a: Usha sees a friend handling nerves on purpose and gives a whisper of encouragement, which suggests Usha felt supportive.

grounding: A student expects nerves, notices a shaky voice after the first slide and slows down, pauses and sips water.

subtype: Approach: reviewing feedback and adjusting for next time [Revision]
passage: After the talk at the university in Manchester, Daniel found two classmates near the coffee machine. "Can I ask you something? What was unclear?" Mateo thought for a moment. "I liked it. But I only understood what you found when you got to the last slide. Before that I was guessing." The other listener nodded. Daniel felt a small sting, then curiosity. The main result had been sitting in the final minute, behind all the methods. That evening Daniel opened the slides, moved the result to slide three, and marked it with a big number. Next time the talk would start with the answer and then explain how it was reached. Mateo received a message: "Thanks. Very useful."

qa.q: Where in the talk had the main result been?
qa.a: The main result had been in the final minute, on the last slide.

qa.q: What did Daniel feel on hearing that the result came too late?
qa.a: Daniel felt a small sting first and then curiosity, which led to changing the slides.

qa.q: What other approach could help Daniel check the change, and why?
qa.a: Daniel could ask the same two listeners to hear the new order, because they can say if the point arrives earlier.

qa.q: How might Mateo see the talk before the result was moved?
qa.a: Mateo said the listening was like guessing, so the audience was probably lost until the last slide. 🙂

grounding: After a talk, a student asks two listeners what was unclear, learns the result was buried and moves it earlier next time.
